questions.prompt: What does the basic exception-safety guarantee promise if a member function throws an exception?
options: All modified objects automatically roll back to their exact pre-call values
No resources are leaked and all class invariants remain intact, though values may have changed
The function is implicitly marked noexcept and calls std::terminate on error
Only stack-allocated primitives are rolled back while heap memory may leak
questions.explanation: The basic guarantee requires zero resource leaks and preserved invariants so surviving objects remain valid and destructible, without promising value rollback (which is the strong guarantee).

questions.prompt: Why does std::vector::push_back copy elements instead of moving them during buffer reallocation when a copyable type's move constructor lacks noexcept?
options: The standard forbids calling non-noexcept move constructors anywhere in <vector>
Copy constructors are always faster than move constructors for small buffers
Moving irreversibly alters the source buffer, so throwing mid-reallocation would break push_back's strong guarantee
Non-noexcept move constructors make std::is_move_constructible_v<S> false
questions.explanation: std::vector uses std::move_if_noexcept to preserve its strong exception-safety guarantee on reallocation: if moving element i can throw, the old elements are already mutated, preventing rollback. When copy construction is available, vector falls back to copying.

questions.prompt: In the snippet below, what happens if Foo's second member initializer (b(arg)) throws an exception?
options: ~A() runs to destroy the completed subobject, and ~Foo() does not run
~Foo() runs first, followed by ~A()
Neither ~A() nor ~Foo() runs because Foo never finished constructing
Both ~B() and ~A() run in reverse declaration order
questions.explanation: An object's lifetime begins only when its constructor completes. When b(arg) throws, b never began lifetime and Foo never finished construction, so ~Foo() and ~B() are skipped—only already-constructed subobjects (a) are destroyed in reverse order.

questions.prompt: Why did C++17 introduce int std::uncaught_exceptions() to replace bool std::uncaught_exception()?
options: uncaught_exception() returned false inside noexcept functions
uncaught_exception() had a data race across threads
uncaught_exceptions() automatically suppresses secondary exceptions thrown in destructors
A boolean cannot distinguish a new inner exception from an outer unwind already active when a scope guard was constructed
questions.explanation: If a RAII transaction guard is constructed inside a catch block or destructor during an outer unwind, uncaught_exception() is already true throughout its scope. Comparing exit count against entry count via std::uncaught_exceptions() accurately detects new unwinding.

questions.prompt: In modern C++ (C++11 and later), what is the implicit exception specification of TrackedHolder::~TrackedHolder() below?
options: noexcept(true), because all destructors are unconditionally noexcept
Potentially throwing (noexcept(false)), inherited from member subobject Tracked::~Tracked()
Ill-formed because a defaulted destructor cannot contain a throwing member
noexcept(true) unless TrackedHolder also holds a virtual base
questions.explanation: Per [class.dtor] and [except.spec], a destructor with no explicit noexcept specifier has the same exception specification as an implicitly declared one—which is noexcept(true) ONLY if all direct base and non-static member destructors are non-throwing. Tracked::~Tracked() is noexcept(false), making ~TrackedHolder() potentially throwing too.

questions.prompt: What happens when execution reaches the closing brace of the catch block in Wrapper's constructor function-try-block?
options: Wrapper finishes constructing with w left uninitialized
The caught exception is swallowed and Wrapper throws std::bad_exception
The currently handled exception is implicitly rethrown
std::terminate() is called unconditionally
questions.explanation: Under [except.handle], if control reaches the end of a handler of a function-try-block on a constructor or destructor without exiting via throw, the current exception is automatically rethrown—a constructor cannot recover and produce a half-constructed object.
